title: Shadow metric anomaly examples (how quality metrics can mislead + mitigations)
body:
Purpose
This doc is a grab-bag of “real-ish” examples we’ve seen in internal replay + early shadow dogfood where quality deltas looked scary (or looked great) but were either (a) artifacts of metric definition, (b) sampling/segmentation quirks, or (c) behavior changes that are not necessarily “quality”.

Use this when:
- A quality metric trips an alert but PM/Eng says “the outputs look fine”.
- A candidate variant “wins” on the dashboard but example review feels worse.
- We see conflicting movement between multiple metrics (e.g., instruction-following up, format adherence down).

Not a spec. This is a debugging and interpretation guide.

Assumptions / current v1 metric set (context)
- Mix of heuristics + model-graded rubric templates (eval-harness) tied to rubric version.
- Default reporting: delta vs control with confidence interval + sample size; segment filters allowed.
- Shadow traffic is fail-open; scoring is async; some missingness is expected.


Anomaly 1 — Format drift looks like a quality regression, but it’s just “extra text”
Scenario
- Control returns JSON only (or function call only).
- Candidate begins adding a natural language preamble: “Sure—here’s the JSON: …” and still returns valid JSON later.

What you see
- Format adherence metric (strict) drops sharply (e.g., 98% → 55%).
- “Tool call success” may also drop if we require exact start token '{' or exact schema wrapper.
- Human review: “the JSON is there; why is this a regression?”

Root cause(s)
- Strict parser expects the entire response to parse as JSON, not “contains JSON”.
- Streaming chunk boundaries can exacerbate: first chunk has preamble, parser fails before full buffer captured.

How to validate quickly
- Open example drilldown; compare raw outputs side-by-side.
- Check whether failures cluster on streaming routes.
- Run “extract-then-parse” offline on a sample to see whether JSON exists and is valid.

Mitigations / improvements
- Provide 2 metrics:
  - strict_json_parse_success
  - json_present_and_parseable (extract JSON block, then parse)
- For streaming shadow capture, score on final concatenated buffer if available; if partial, mark as “unscorable” rather than “fail”.
- UI guidance: if strict drops but “present+parseable” stays flat, treat as formatting preference change (could still matter for downstream clients).


Anomaly 2 — Verbosity increases inflate “helpfulness” / rubric scores while hurting user experience
Scenario
- Candidate is more verbose, adds caveats, longer step-by-step answers.

What you see
- Model-graded “helpfulness” or “completeness” rubric improves.
- Latency/cost increases (expected).
- Customer complains outputs feel “rambling”.

Root cause(s)
- Rubric prompt rewards coverage and detail; does not penalize concision.
- Judge model may have its own verbosity bias.

How to validate quickly
- Plot delta of output_tokens and helpfulness score. Look for positive correlation.
- Segment by route intent: “short answer” endpoints vs “analysis” endpoints.
- Run a small human spot-check on top 20 examples with largest helpfulness gains.

Mitigations / improvements
- Add explicit concision/verbosity metric:
  - verbosity_ratio = output_tokens / expected_tokens (expected defined per route or via baseline quantiles)
  - or “excess_tokens_above_p95_control”
- Update helpfulness rubric template to include: “Prefer concise answers when user asks for concise; penalize unnecessary verbosity.”
- Alerting rule should not page purely on rubric movement without checking tokens and route intent.


Anomaly 3 — “Refusal rate” changes are driven by safer preambles, not real refusal behavior
Scenario
- Candidate adds safety disclaimers more often (e.g., “I can’t help with that, but…”), but still provides allowed help.

What you see
- Refusal rate increases (heuristic keyword-based).
- Safety rubric score may improve or stay flat.
- Example review: it’s not refusing; it’s hedging.

Root cause(s)
- Heuristic refusal detector triggered by phrases like “I can’t”, “I’m not able to”, “I cannot provide”.
- Model uses “I can’t” as a stylistic intro even when providing answer.

How to validate quickly
- Compare heuristic refusal flags vs model-graded refusal rubric.
- Review flagged examples; check for “refusal then comply” patterns.

Mitigations / improvements
- Replace naive keyword refusal with structured classifier or judge rubric:
  - refusal = “does the assistant ultimately withhold the requested allowed info?”
- For v1 heuristics, add “refusal_then_compliance” separate metric.
- In UI, show “heuristic_refusal_rate” vs “rubric_refusal_rate” and explain mismatch.


Anomaly 4 — Faithfulness proxy improves because candidate is more vague
Scenario
- Candidate stops making specific claims; answers become generic.

What you see
- “Hallucination” or “faithfulness proxy” improves (fewer named entities, fewer numeric claims).
- Instruction-following drops (“be specific”, “cite sources”), or user satisfaction drops.

Root cause(s)
- Proxy metrics often detect risky patterns (numbers, entities) rather than true correctness.
- Vague outputs evade penalties.

How to validate quickly
- Check named_entity_rate / numeric_claim_rate alongside faithfulness proxy.
- Inspect examples with largest proxy improvements; see if answers became evasive.

Mitigations / improvements
- Pair faithfulness proxy with specificity metric:
  - entities_per_100_tokens
  - number_of_grounded_citations (if citations are part of format)
- For judge rubric, include a criterion: “Answer is specific and addresses user request, not evasive.”


Anomaly 5 — “Instruction following” metric drops due to harmless reordering
Scenario
- Prompt asks for “1) summary 2) steps 3) caveats” and candidate outputs “steps first, summary second” but includes all parts.

What you see
- Heuristic “format adherence” fails.
- Judge “instruction following” may drop if it expects exact order.

Root cause(s)
- Overly rigid rubric/heuristic on ordering rather than presence.

How to validate quickly
- Compare “section_presence” (does it include all requested sections) vs “order_exact”.
- Review examples with failures; classify: missing vs reordered.

Mitigations / improvements
- Split metrics: presence vs order.
- In rubric, allow order-insensitive matching unless prompt explicitly says “in this order”.


Anomaly 6 — Metrics swing because shadow capture truncates outputs (streaming edge case)
Scenario
- Shadow path times out or stops capturing after N tokens/chunks; control path completes.

What you see
- Candidate appears to have worse instruction following / format adherence.
- Output_tokens in shadow are systematically lower.
- Scoring lag increases; missing scores increase.

Root cause(s)
- Shadow capture termination semantics differ from control.
- Aggressive timeouts/circuit breaker for shadow.

How to validate quickly
- Plot distribution of shadow_output_tokens vs control_output_tokens for same request fingerprint.
- Check shadow capture status fields (timeout, truncated, completed).

Mitigations / improvements
- Scoring should treat truncated outputs as “invalid_for_quality” unless metric is specifically about first-N tokens.
- Dashboards should default to excluding “truncated” from quality denominator and show truncation rate separately.
- If truncation rate rises above threshold, page SRE (this is a pipeline correctness issue).


Anomaly 7 — A/B bucketing + sampling produces Simpson’s paradox (aggregate delta flips sign)
Scenario
- Candidate performs better on one customer segment but worse on another.
- Sampling rate differs by route or tenant due to quotas.

What you see
- Overall delta shows improvement.
- High-value route shows regression when filtered.

Root cause(s)
- Non-uniform sampling or missingness interacts with segment composition.
- Candidate might be routed more on “easy” traffic if shadow policy isn’t uniform across request types.

How to validate quickly
- Always check deltas by: route, request_type (chat vs completions vs tools), model_context_length_bucket.
- Confirm deterministic bucketing is stable and identical for control/shadow comparison.

Mitigations / improvements
- Require per-segment minimum sample sizes before surfacing strong conclusions.
- Add “composition” panel in Console: top segment shares in control vs shadow sample.
- Where possible, compare paired samples by request_fingerprint (paired analysis) rather than independent aggregates.


Anomaly 8 — Judge drift / rubric version changes look like model regressions
Scenario
- We update judge model or rubric template between runs.

What you see
- Big shift in rubric-based metrics across time even without a model change.

Root cause(s)
- Rubric prompt changes or judge model change.
- Calibration thresholds adjusted.

How to validate quickly
- Confirm rubric_version and judge_model_version pinned per experiment.
- Compare metrics for a fixed “anchor prompt set” scored by both versions.

Mitigations / improvements
- Enforce rubric version pinning per experiment (and display prominently).
- Add a “rubric version changed” banner on charts.
- Keep an internal calibration dataset and publish judge drift notes before rollout.


Anomaly 9 — PII redaction transforms the prompt and changes scoring outcomes
Scenario
- Redaction removes emails/account numbers; candidate vs control may differ in sensitivity to missing tokens.

What you see
- Metrics computed on redacted prompt show changes that don’t match user experience.

Root cause(s)
- We score on redacted artifacts, not raw prompt.
- Redaction can remove key instruction tokens (false positives) or collapse structure.

How to validate quickly
- Review redaction logs on flagged examples: what was removed, what regex triggered.
- Compare rubric scores on raw (internal-only safe dataset) vs redacted for a small sample.

Mitigations / improvements
- Prefer structured allowlists (fields to keep) over regex-heavy redaction when possible.
- Add redaction quality metric: fraction_tokens_redacted; redaction_trigger_count.
- In regulated environments, we may accept reduced metric fidelity; be explicit in docs.


Anomaly 10 — “Safety” improves because candidate over-refuses, but heuristic safety looks fine
Scenario
- Candidate refuses borderline safe content more often.

What you see
- Harmful content rate drops (judge says “safe”).
- Refusal rate increases.
- Customer goals for allowed content are impacted.

Root cause(s)
- Safety metric is one-sided; it doesn’t capture “over-refusal” cost.

How to validate quickly
- Add allowed-content benchmark prompts (internal or customer-provided prompt set) to measure false positives.
- Compare refusal rate specifically on “allowed” labeled slices.

Mitigations / improvements
- Track both:
  - unsafe_compliance_rate
  - over_refusal_rate (refusal on allowed prompts)
- For production shadow traffic, approximate with heuristics on intent categories if labels aren’t available.


Anomaly 11 — Tiny denominators and multiple comparisons create “phantom regressions”
Scenario
- We view many metrics across many segments; some will look significant by chance.

What you see
- One metric/segment shows a scary delta with wide CI.

Root cause(s)
- Low sample sizes; p-hacking style effect from many charts.

How to validate quickly
- Check sample size + CI width.
- Confirm alert policy uses minimum N and correction (or at least a more conservative threshold).

Mitigations / improvements
- Hard minimum samples before alerting (per segment).
- Prefer sequential testing / always-valid bounds for “auto-stop” and “auto-rollback” later; for v1 keep signals advisory.


Anomaly 12 — Candidate improves “exact match” on evaluation harness, but degrades in production due to tool availability differences
Scenario
- Offline eval harness assumes tools/functions available; production route has tool restrictions or different schemas.

What you see
- Offline quality results look strong.
- Shadow traffic shows tool-call errors or format issues.

Root cause(s)
- Mismatch between eval harness environment and production route config.

How to validate quickly
- Compare tool schema versions, allowed tool list, and “tool_choice” policy between eval harness run and route.

Mitigations / improvements
- Attach route config snapshot (tool schema hash, prompt template version) to shadow experiment metadata.
- Provide “environment parity” checks when creating an experiment.


Operational checklist when a metric looks “wrong”
1) Check capture integrity: truncated/timeouts? missingness? scoring lag?
2) Check token deltas: output_tokens and stop_reason distributions.
3) Check rubric pinning: rubric_version and judge_model_version.
4) Split strict vs lenient metrics (parse success vs parseable after extraction).
5) Segment before concluding: route, request_type, ctx_length buckets, streaming vs non-streaming.
6) Review top examples by metric contribution (not random).
7) If still unclear, run quick offline re-score on a small sample with alternative rubric.


Notes / TODOs
- Add a small “anomaly gallery” to Console help panel (Kenji asked for tooltip content) with 3–5 common patterns: verbosity, strict JSON, truncation, rubric drift.
- We should standardize denominators: for each metric, define whether denominator excludes truncated/unscorable.
- Need explicit label for “heuristic metric” vs “judge metric” in dashboards (reduce trust confusion).

Appendix: suggested metric additions (v1.1-ish)
- response_truncated_rate
- json_present_and_parseable (lenient)
- verbosity_ratio + p95 token delta
- fraction_tokens_redacted
- refusal_then_compliance_rate
- specificity proxy (entities_per_100_tokens)
